column2: Homage to you, who are in all beings, to the one with a bell in hand; homage to the five-faced god, to the lord of the fields.
Homage to the primal support of all beings, the bearer of the earth, of many forms, without qualities, the Supreme Self.
Homage to the lord of the staff, to the lord of the hosts (ganas); homage to Hiranyagarbha, to the lord of gold.
Homage to you of golden seed, golden-armed; homage to the one whose form is meditation, witness of meditation.
Homage to you who abide in meditation, who are reached by meditation, by whom this entire universe of moving and unmoving things shines,
produced like rain from a cloud, in the form of Prakriti and Purusha.
The self-luminous great Self, the supreme eternal light, whom the knowers of truth call the sun, the eye of men;
the lord of Uma, Nandikesha, the blue-throated, ever-auspicious Shiva, conqueror of death, Mahadeva, higher than the highest, all-pervading:
the supreme, of the form of the Word-Brahman, cause of all — I praise him. Homage to you of matted hair; homage to the one born at once (Sadyojata).
To the source of existence, the pure, the eldest and the youngest; to wrath, to desire, lord of the three, thread of sacrifice;
to energy, lord of the directions, to Time of the Aghora form, to you whose seed is fire — homage to the great-souled.
From whom come the oceans, rivers and mountains, hosts of Gandharvas, Yakshas, Asuras and Siddhas, the fixed and the moving, the great and the small, being and non-being, the living —
I bow to him whose lotus feet the yogis worship, the Self within all, the formless Lord, the independent One, the quality of the qualified; again and again I bow.
Thus praised, Mahadeva Shankara, the benefactor of the world, appeared before the king, who was heated by his austerity.
With five faces and ten arms, a crescent moon for crest, three-eyed, of noble limbs, with a snake for sacred thread,
broad-chested, bright as the snowy mountain, clad in elephant-hide, his lotus feet worshipped by the gods —
seeing him, O Narada, the king fell at his feet like a staff on the ground; then rising quickly, he stood before Shiva with folded hands,
and bowed to Mahadeva, chanting the name Shankara. Knowing the king's devotion, Shankara, crowned with the moon,
said to the king: "I am pleased; choose the boon you desire. I am pleased with you by your hymn and austerity."
Thus addressed by the god, the king, contented in mind, folded his hands and said to the Lord of lords of the worlds:
Bhagiratha said: "If I am to be favoured by a boon, O Maheshvara, then give the Ganga for the liberation of my ancestors."
Shri Shiva said: "I have given you the Ganga; your ancestors have the highest goal, and you liberation." Having said so, Shiva vanished.
Terrified, the Ganga, the one purifier of the worlds, was held in his matted locks; purifying the whole world, she followed Bhagiratha.
From then on that goddess, stainless, remover of stains, was famed in the three worlds as Bhagirathi, O sage.
The best of rivers, the Ganga, flooded the place where Sagara's sons had formerly been burned for their sin.
At the very moment the ashes of the Sagara sons were drenched by the Ganga, they were lifted from hell, their sins gone.
Those who had been terribly tormented by Yama and cried out were honoured by him now, drenched in Ganga water.
Knowing the sons of Sagara to be free of sin, Yama bowed to them and honoured them as prescribed, and said with a pleased mind:
O sons of the king, you are freed from this very dreadful hell; board the aerial car and go to Vishnu's abode.
Thus addressed by Yama, those great souls, their sins gone, took divine bodies and went to the world of Vishnu.
Such is the power of that Ganga, born from the tip of Vishnu's foot, famed in all the worlds as the destroyer of great sins.
Whoever reads or hears this holy account that destroys great sins gains the fruit of bathing in the Ganga.
He who tells this holy account before Brahmins goes to Vishnu's abode, from which there is no return.
Having finished the vigil and rites, he should give to a knower of the Self two and a half measures of wheat and a fee in gold according to his means.
Homage to you, Hrishikesha, sole cause of all the worlds; by this gift of wheat, give me all happiness.
He should feed Brahmins as he can, and himself eat silently. Freed from all sins, he gains the fruit of the Brahmamedha.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Ashvina, having fasted on the twelfth day, the pure devotee should bathe Padmanabha with milk with devotion.
Homage to Padmanabha — he should make an oblation as he is able, and worship properly with sesame, rice, barley and ghee.
Having kept the night's vigil, he should perform the worship again, and give to a Brahmin a measure of honey with a fee.
Homage to you, Padmanabha, grandfather of all the worlds; pleased with this gift of honey, be the giver of all happiness.
The wise man who with devotion keeps the Padmanabha vow obtains, certainly, the fruit of a thousand Brahmamedhas.
On the twelfth of the bright half of Kartika, fasting and self-controlled, with a measure of milk, curds and ghee in the same quantity,
with "Homage to Damodara" he should bathe him with devotion; having offered a hundred and eight oblations of honey, ghee and sesame,
he should keep a controlled vigil, intent on worship three times; in the morning he should worship the god with lovely lotus flowers.
Again he should offer a hundred and eight oblations with ghee and sesame, and with devotion give a Brahmin food with five kinds of dishes.
O Damodara, Lord of the world, cause of the cause of all, save me by your mercy, O god, protector of those who seek refuge.
With this he should give a gift to a Vedic scholar who is a householder, give a fee as he is able, and feed Brahmins.
Having thus done the vow well, he should eat with his kinsmen; he gains double the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
The observer who does this best twelfth-day vow for a year, O best of sages, goes to the highest state.
Whoever does it with devotion for one month or two obtains that fruit and attains Hari's abode.
Having completed a full year, the observer should perform the conclusion on the twelfth of the dark half of Margashirsha, O lord of sages.
Having bathed in the morning, cleaned his teeth as per custom, wearing white garlands and garments, anointed with white fragrance,
he should have a lovely square pavilion built, with bells and chowries, adorned with the sound of little bells,
decorated with garlands of flowers, shining with canopy and banners, covered with white cloth, adorned with rows of lamps.
In its middle he should make a well-adorned "sarvatobhadra" diagram, and on it place twelve pots filled with water.
All the pots, with the five gems, should be covered with a single well-purified cloth.
The devotee should have an image of the god Lakshmi-Narayana made of gold, silver or copper, O Brahmins,
and the self-controlled one should place the image on the pots, or its value in gold according to his means, O best of Brahmins.
In all vows the wise should avoid stinginess with wealth; if he does it, his life, wealth and prosperity decline.
Full of devotion, he should first bathe the god Narayana, reclining on Ananta, the faultless, with the five nectars.
He should offer the services with the names beginning with Keshava; at night he should keep vigil with hearing of the Puranas and the like.
Having conquered sleep, fasting well, controlling the senses, he should worship the god three times, with ritual as his means allow.
Then, rising in the morning and finishing the morning rites, he should have Brahmins offer a thousand sesame oblations with the sacred utterances.
Then he should worship the god in order with fragrance, flowers and so on, and before the god hear the Purana.
He should give twelve Brahmins curd-rice and milk-rice, with ten cakes, with ghee and a fee.
O god of gods, Lord of the world, whose form favours devotees, accept this offering, Krishna, and be the giver of all desires.
Having given the offering with this, he should pray standing with folded hands, with knees on the ground, bowed in humility.
Homage, homage to you, king of the kings of the gods; homage to you, God, dwelling of the world; make my vow today fully fruitful; homage to you, Supreme Person.
Thus he should pray to the Brahmins and to the Supreme Person, and offer water of welcome to the god together with Mahalakshmi.
Homage to you, Lord of Lakshmi, dweller in the Milk Ocean; accept the offering, O Lord of the gods, together with Lakshmi.
I praise Achyuta, by whose remembrance and name any deficiency in austerity, sacrifice and rites at once becomes complete.
Having thus petitioned the Lord of gods, the self-controlled observer should present the image with a fee to the teacher.
Afterward he should feed Brahmins and give a fee according to his power; then he should eat silently with his kinsmen.
In the evening he should hear Vishnu's stories with the learned. The man who does this twelfth-day vow
obtains all desires here and hereafter, O Narada; with three hundred family members, free of all sins, he goes to Vishnu's abode, from which one does not grieve.
